I have enough evidence now to draft a conclusion.

## Conclusion

The claim that increasing the number of childhood vaccines causes autism is **not supported by scientific evidence**. This specific hypothesis—that cumulative vaccine antigen exposure overwhelms a child's immune system and triggers autism—was directly tested by DeStefano et al. (2013) in *The Journal of Pediatrics*, a large case-control study comparing total vaccine antigens received by children with and without autism. It found **no association** between antigen quantity and autism risk, even though today's schedule contains more vaccines than in the 1990s (https://www.jpeds.com/article/S0022-3476(13)00666-5/fulltext; summarized at https://www.npr.org/sections/health-shots/2013/03/29/175626824/the-number-of-early-childhood-vaccines-not-linked-to-autism).

This finding aligns with the broader scientific consensus. The Institute of Medicine's comprehensive 2004 review concluded evidence favors rejecting a causal link between vaccines (with or without thimerosal) and autism (https://www.nationalacademies.org/publications/10997). A 2021 review in *Vaccine* similarly notes the "great majority" of scientists, physicians, and public health researchers have refuted vaccine-autism causation after extensive scrutiny (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1090379821002312).

Note: in 2025 the CDC controversially revised its own website language, claiming the "vaccines do not cause autism" statement isn't "evidence-based." Independent fact-checkers found this revision misrepresents the underlying research, including misreading aluminum-adjuvant studies that actually contradict a vaccine-autism link (https://www.factcheck.org/2025/11/revised-cdc-website-about-autism-and-vaccines-is-not-evidence-based/).

**Bottom line:** Multiple large, peer-reviewed studies directly testing this claim—including one specifically examining vaccine quantity/antigen load—find no causal relationship between the number of childhood vaccines and autism risk.
